strengths: Novel and well-motivated bilevel reformulation: casting differentiable optimization as a bilevel problem and introducing an active-set Lagrangian/ghost-problem construction to reduce general convex constraints to a linear-equality surrogate is a clean idea that extends prior first-order bilevel results (Kornowski et al., 2024) from equality-only to inequality-constrained settings.

Solid theoretical development: the paper provides an active-set equivalence theorem, a finite-difference hypergradient approximation with explicit O(δ) error bound, and a convergence result matching the best-known O~(δ^-1 ε^-3) rate for nonsmooth nonconvex stationarity, plus an extension to general convex constraints (Appendix D) under additional 'well-behaved' assumptions.

Honest and rigorous treatment of a key limitation: rather than silently assuming perfect active-set identification, the authors construct an explicit hardness example (Appendix F, Lemma F.1) showing why the assumption is needed, and provide a randomized-smoothing algorithm that removes the assumption at a corresponding cost — this is a commendable level of rigor rarely seen in limitations discussions.

Practically valuable solver-agnostic design: the reformulation of the perturbation as a linear term via a stop-gradient trick (Section 5) enables true black-box compatibility with GUROBI/MOSEK/SCS without custom backward passes, addressing a genuine practical need in the differentiable-optimization ecosystem.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three qualitatively different tasks (synthetic DFL/QP, Sudoku/LP, SOCP) against six baselines spanning KKT-based and optimization-based families, with convergence, runtime, memory, gradient-fidelity (cosine similarity), batch-size, and tolerance ablations.

Demonstrated scalability advantages: near-constant memory usage and sublinear runtime growth versus CvxpyLayer's superlinear growth and eventual OOM, which is a meaningful practical contribution for large-scale decision-focused learning pipelines.
weaknesses: The core theoretical guarantees rest on fairly strong assumptions (LICQ, μg-strong convexity of the lower-level objective, exact/near-exact active-set identification, well-conditioned solves achievable in O(log 1/ε) time) that may not hold for many practical convex programs (e.g., plain LPs without regularization); the paper partially compensates for the active-set assumption but the strong-convexity and LICQ assumptions are used throughout without much discussion of how often they fail in practice.

The claimed O(log(1/ε)) hypergradient complexity is stated in terms of oracle/gradient evaluations assuming the underlying convex solves converge geometrically to the target tolerance; this treats the per-solve cost as a black box and may understate real computational cost for large or ill-conditioned lower-level problems, somewhat overstating the 'near-constant' framing in the abstract.

Algorithm 1 requires two full solves per hypergradient (original + perturbed problem), and it is not clearly discussed how sensitive overall wall-clock is to warm-starting or how the perturbation magnitude δ is chosen/tuned in practice beyond δ=O(ε); no explicit ablation is given for the interaction between δ choice and gradient bias/variance beyond the tolerance ablation.
One key baseline (BPQP) is self-implemented rather than using an official release, which raises reproducibility and fairness concerns for the runtime comparisons in Figure 4 and Figure 10.

The gradient cosine-similarity ablation (Figure 11) shows non-trivial dips (down to ~0.5–0.6) during training for some dimensions, suggesting the approximate hypergradient can meaningfully deviate from the true gradient at certain training stages; this is not thoroughly analyzed or connected back to the theoretical O(δ) bound.

Experiments are restricted to synthetic/small-scale benchmarks (synthetic DFL, Sudoku, synthetic SOCP); there is no evaluation on established real-world decision-focused learning or control benchmarks, limiting evidence for significance/impact in realistic settings.

The source code URL is left blank in the manuscript ('source code is available at'), which, combined with the self-implemented baseline, somewhat weakens the reproducibility of the empirical claims as presented.

The extension to general convex constraints (Appendix D) is only proven under an additional black-box 'approximate dual oracle' assumption whose practical instantiation/algorithm is not concretely specified, making the generality claim ("general convex constraints") in the main text slightly stronger than what is rigorously established.

strengths: Novel and conceptually appealing reformulation of the KKT/implicit-differentiation problem as a bilevel optimization instance, with a well-motivated active-set Lagrangian ('ghost problem') that converts inequality constraints into a locally equivalent equality-constrained surrogate.

Non-trivial theoretical contribution: extends the O(log(1/ε)) equality-only hypergradient rate of Kornowski et al. (2024) to the inequality-constrained setting, and further extends guarantees to general (well-behaved) convex constraints, addressing an open problem raised in prior work.

Practical, solver-agnostic implementation (drop-in replacement for CvxpyLayer) that lets the method leverage state-of-the-art commercial solvers (GUROBI, MOSEK) without solver-specific backward passes -- a genuinely useful engineering contribution.

Reasonably thorough experimental study across three task types (DFL/QP, Sudoku/LP, SOCP), with runtime, memory, and scalability comparisons against six baselines, plus multiple ablations (batch size, tolerance, gradient cosine similarity, GPU comparison) in the appendix.

Honest acknowledgment in the paper (Table 1, Appendix F) that the method returns only an ε-approximate hypergradient and that active-set identification is a necessary, non-trivial assumption, along with an attempt (Theorem F.2) to remove this assumption via smoothing at some rate cost.
weaknesses: The central theoretical results (Theorem 4.6, Corollary 4.7) rely heavily on Assumption 4.3 (exact active-set identification), which is essentially assumed rather than derived; the paper's own counterexample (Appendix F, Lemma F.1) shows the problem is discontinuous/ill-posed without it, undermining confidence that the headline O(log(1/ε)) rate is attainable in realistic settings where the active set is only approximately known. The randomized fix (Theorem F.2) that removes this assumption sacrifices exactness/rate clarity and is relegated to an appendix without empirical validation.

The method never produces an exact hypergradient (marked with a dagger in Table 1 versus several baselines that do), which is a real practical downgrade from KKT-based approaches when high-fidelity gradients matter; the paper does not quantify how large the resulting training or generalization bias can be beyond a few cosine-similarity plots.

The backward pass requires solving an additional perturbed lower-level problem from scratch at every step (Eq. 7), effectively doubling the number of full solver calls compared to standard implicit differentiation; the 'near-constant O(log(1/ε))' framing can obscure this practically significant constant-factor overhead, and no experiment isolates this cost from the reduced Hessian-factorization savings.

Runtime/memory advantages over CvxpyLayer appear substantially driven by CVXPY's cone-program canonicalization overhead rather than a like-for-like comparison of the differentiation algorithm itself; a baseline that isolates canonicalization from differentiation cost is largely missing, weakening the causal attribution of the reported gains to the proposed hypergradient oracle.

Despite stating 10 random seeds were used, the main convergence plots (Figure 3) show single curves with no variance or error bars, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported convergence-matching and speed claims.

The LPGD baseline comparison appears potentially unfavorable to LPGD: the authors note its default tolerance was insufficient and then report results after tightening its tolerance to 1e-12, which produces a large runtime penalty for LPGD, while the proposed method uses much looser tolerances; this asymmetric tuning protocol could bias the comparison.

The general convex-constraint theory (Appendix D) requires several additional strong assumptions (approximate oracle with matching active set, Hessian-smoothness, bounded dual norms) whose applicability to the SOCP experiments is not explicitly verified, leaving a gap between the theoretical guarantees and the empirical SOCP results in Section 6.3.

Part of the convergence-rate contribution is obtained by combining the existing meta-algorithm of Kornowski et al. (2024) with the paper's improved oracle rather than a fundamentally new convergence-analysis technique, making the overall theoretical advance somewhat incremental relative to prior first-order bilevel optimization work.

strengths: Introduces a novel and elegant bilevel reformulation of differentiable optimization layers, using an active-set Lagrangian ('ghost problem') that reduces general convex constraints to a locally equivalent equality-constrained surrogate, enabling O(log(1/ϵ)) hypergradient approximation instead of the O(1/ϵ) rate of prior penalty-based bilevel methods.

Theoretical contributions are non-trivial and carefully proved (Theorem 4.5 active-set equivalence, finite-difference error bound in Lemma C.1, and extension from linear to general convex constraints in Appendix D), and the paper explicitly discusses why the active-set assumption is necessary via a clean hardness counterexample (Lemma F.1), which is commendable honesty about limitations.

The method is implemented as a genuinely solver-agnostic, drop-in PyTorch/CVXPY layer (Figure 2) compatible with commercial solvers like GUROBI/MOSEK, which is a practically valuable engineering contribution absent from most competing first-order methods.

Experiments span multiple problem classes (QP-based DFL, Sudoku LP, SOCP) and multiple axes of comparison (convergence, wall-clock forward/backward time, memory scaling, batch size, tolerance sensitivity, gradient cosine similarity vs. ground truth), providing a fairly comprehensive empirical picture.

Scalability results (Figures 5-7) are compelling: near-constant memory and sub-linear time growth versus CvxpyLayer's rapid superlinear growth and OOM failures, directly supporting the paper's central motivating claim.
weaknesses: The core efficiency and correctness guarantees rest on Assumption 4.3 (active-set identification) and, in practice, on a heuristic active-set estimate from an approximate black-box solve; the paper's own Lemma F.1 shows that no continuous hypergradient estimator can be accurate without such an assumption, meaning behavior near degenerate/boundary active-set transitions in real training could be unreliable, and the fallback smoothed algorithm in Theorem F.2 (which removes the assumption) is not the one used in the main experiments/implementation.

For general convex constraints (Appendix D), the O(log(1/ϵ)) type guarantee (Corollary D.5) depends on Assumption D.1's abstract 'approximate dual oracle' whose existence/complexity for general convex constraints is not concretely established, so the headline Õ(δ⁻¹ϵ⁻³) rate for the general convex setting is not fully algorithmically realized, only oracle-complexity bounded.

FFOLayer explicitly returns an approximate (not exact) hypergradient (Table 1, '✗†'), and no error-vs-downstream-training-quality analysis (beyond cosine similarity plots) is provided for cases where active-set misidentification could occur, e.g. near constraint boundaries during early/unstable training.

All experiments are run on CPU only due to lack of batch GPU solvers, and benchmarks are limited to synthetic/toy tasks (synthetic DFL, Sudoku, SOCP); there is no evaluation on a real-world decision-focused learning benchmark or larger-scale application that would more convincingly demonstrate practical significance.
One baseline (BPQP) is self-implemented rather than using an official release, raising minor reproducibility/fairness concerns for that particular comparison.

The perturbation parameter δ and solver tolerances required to realize the theoretical guarantees are not always straightforward to set in practice (as seen with LPGD's tolerance sensitivity), and the paper does not fully characterize how sensitive FFOLayer itself is to mis-specified δ beyond a limited ablation.
